content: Mumps is a highly contagious disease caused by a virus. Individuals infected with mumps can transmit the virus to others through various means, including coughing, sneezing, or talking. Sharing items contaminated with saliva, such as water bottles or cups, can also spread the virus. Additionally, close-contact activities like playing sports, dancing, or kissing can facilitate transmission. The symptoms of mumps may include fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, loss of appetite, and swelling or tenderness of the salivary glands located under the ears or jaw (a condition known as parotitis). This swelling can occur on one or both sides of the face. While most individuals recover fully from mumps, the infection can occasionally lead to complications. These complications may include inflammation of the brain (encephalitis), testicles (orchitis), ovaries (oophoritis), or breasts (mastitis). In some cases, mumps can result in temporary or permanent hearing loss. Mumps remains prevalent in many countries worldwide. Travelers who are not vaccinated are at an increased risk of contracting the disease. Outbreaks of mumps are more likely to occur in settings where people have frequent and close interactions, such as among college students, sports teams, or members of community groups like churches. Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing mumps. In the United States, the mumps vaccine is routinely administered to children as part of the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) or MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella) combination vaccines. The vaccine is given in two doses: the first dose is typically administered at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second dose is given between 4 and 6 years of age. For individuals born in or after 1957 who have never had mumps or have not been vaccinated, it is recommended to receive two doses of the MMR vaccine before traveling. The second dose should be administered at least 28 days after the first. Infants aged 6 to 11 months who are traveling internationally should receive one dose of the MMR vaccine prior to travel; however, this dose does not count as part of the routine childhood vaccination series. It is important to note that vaccine-induced immunity can wane over time. However, individuals who have been vaccinated and subsequently contract mumps typically experience milder symptoms and are less likely to develop complications. Pregnant individuals should not receive the MMR vaccine. Additionally, anyone who receives the MMR vaccine should avoid becoming pregnant for at least four weeks following vaccination.
